reasons: Lake identity is verified for United States v. Knotts, U.S. Supreme Court, decided 1983-03-02, year 1983.
Lake citations list official 460 U.S. 276, vendor-neutral 1983 U.S. LEXIS 135, and the stated parallels 103 S. Ct. 1081, 75 L. Ed. 2d 55, 51 U.S.L.W. 4232.
The opinion states: “A person traveling in an automobile on public thoroughfares has no reasonable expectation of privacy in his movements from one place to another.”
The opinion concludes that the challenged beeper monitoring invaded no legitimate expectation of privacy and therefore was neither a search nor a seizure.
residual_risks: The holding does not cover beeper installation, interior monitoring, or dragnet-style long-term surveillance.
reviewed.suggested_tightening: For maximum precision, limit the holding to limited public-road tracking that revealed no interior information.

defect.evidence_quote: When he used his phone, [Smith] voluntarily conveyed numerical information to the telephone company and ‘exposed’ that information to its equipment in the ordinary course of business.
defect.problem: The case is supportable only as a related comparator/cross-reference, not as a third-party-doctrine or CSLI holding.
defect.proposed_fix: Change role to “Related comparator — public-movement baseline for CSLI/third-party doctrine; not a CSLI or third-party holding.”

reasons: Knotts analogizes to Smith v. Maryland, which supports a loose cross-reference.
Knotts itself concerns beeper tracking of public automobile movements, not cell-site location information or disclosure of records to a third-party provider.
residual_risks: No disclosed home-page text defines the corpus meaning of this home label.
reviewed.suggested_tightening: Make the role expressly comparative rather than doctrinal.

reasons: The opinion frames the governing inquiry around a reasonable, legitimate, or justifiable expectation of privacy.
The final holding asks whether beeper monitoring invaded a legitimate expectation of privacy and holds it did not.
The case directly concerns officers monitoring a beeper to trace a vehicle carrying chloroform over public roads.
The opinion treats the beeper as technological augmentation of visual surveillance and holds that this public-movement monitoring was not a Fourth Amendment search.
residual_risks: The “anchor” label should remain limited to the public-movements baseline, not interior or installation scenarios.
